transcript:
MEETING HEADER: 2025-08-21 15:00 UTC | Duration: 72m | Attendees: Alyssa Chen (Redwood AE); Mateo Ruiz (Redwood SE); Priya Nair (Redwood); Samir Patel (StratusCare Head Platform); Dana Liu (ML Eng); Mark Rivera (Infra); Olivia Park (PM); Jared Kim (Security)

AUTO SUMMARY (auto-gen, may be incomplete): Align on POC SLOs TTFT/TPOT, sample plan, benchmark runbook, timeline and owners.

TOPICS LISTED: TTFT vs TPOT, p95/p99 targets, traffic shaping, sample sizes, benchmark orchestration, acceptance criteria.

00:00 - Speaker 1 (Alyssa Chen): Hey everybody, thanks for joining. want to run through the scope for the POC, specifically latency targets and how we measure them, and make sure we capture constraints — infra, data, security — up front.
00:22 - Speaker 2 (Samir): Yeah thanks. Quick context from us: StratusCare is instrumenting chat triage across telehealth workflows. Peak qps is modest, about 80 rps with heavy diurnal peaks, but tail latency is the customer pain. We currently see sporadic 95/99 spikes when long context hits and when payloads are large.
00:45 - Speaker 3 (Mateo Ruiz): Helpful. are you running models in-cloud today or is it hybrid?
00:50 - Speaker 4 (Samir): Hybrid. We have a mix, some hosted endpoints on cloud provider and an on-prem inference cluster for PHI. The POC needs to consider both.
01:05 - Speaker 3 (Mateo Ruiz): Good — that affects TTFT more than TPOT usually because network and cold starts matter. Quick question: what does StratusCare consider "first token" for this workflow? Is the UX looking for the first informative token (i.e. answer start) or any non-empty token?
01:20 - Speaker 5 (Olivia Park): For product we'd like first meaningful token — user should see the first chunk in under ~200 ms ideally, otherwise it feels laggy.
01:30 - Speaker 3 (Mateo Ruiz): Okay noted. We'll use the first non-empty token as proxy but we'll also capture first-meaningful via a small human-labeled sample in evaluation.
01:40 - Speaker 2 (Samir): On SLOs, we're thinking p95 and p99 both matter. p99 is the one that kills the UX.
01:46 - Speaker 6 (Jared Kim): From security side we need audit logs and proof that no PHI leaves the private cluster during those runs. Also KMS / envelope encryption for keys in dedicated runs.
02:05 - Speaker 1 (Alyssa Chen): We'll include attestation steps and a checklist for the private run. On the performance side, propose we split SLOs into two orthogonal metrics: TTFT (time to first token) and TPOT (per-token throughput/time per token).
02:20 - Speaker 3 (Mateo Ruiz): Right. TTFT covers initial latency — network, cold-start, model load — and TPOT captures steady-state generation speed (ms/token). For multi-turn chat, both matter: initial reply responsiveness and sustained streaming.
02:35 - Speaker 4 (Dana Liu): Our median response is about 6 tokens to first meaningful word? hmm, I mean median length of initial chunk. Most generation runs 150-300 tokens total. Sequence length distribution: 8% very long (>1024), 60% medium (256-1024), 32% short (<256).
02:55 - Speaker 3 (Mateo Ruiz): Great, we'll parameterize tests by three buckets: short/med/long. Benchmarks should weight traffic by your actual distribution.
03:05 - Speaker 1 (Alyssa Chen): Let's talk numbers — rough targets to align on. We usually propose baseline TTFT p95 150 ms, p99 350 ms on hosted Redwood for a shorter prompt and an optimized model. TPOT per-token p95 25 ms, p99 70 ms for steady generation on GPU with batching; but those numbers vary a lot by model size and quantization. Thoughts?
03:25 - Speaker 5 (Olivia Park): 150 p95 is ambitious but acceptable as aspirational; product can tolerate occasional >200 if p99 under 400. We should be explicit about sequence length assumptions.
03:35 - Speaker 4 (Dana Liu): Our production SLO request: p95 TTFT <= 200ms, p99 TTFT <= 450ms; TPOT p95 <= 40ms, p99 <= 100ms. If you can hit that with our medium-weighted mix we'll consider it a pass.
03:55 - Speaker 3 (Mateo Ruiz): That's useful. We'll map those back to hardware profiles. Note: for private on-prem with network hops and possible NVMe model load we may need relaxed targets. We'll capture separate acceptance bands: hosted vs private.
04:15 - Speaker 6 (Jared Kim): Also call out confidentiality — we need local metrics capture only, and Redwood must provide a portable measurement harness so we can run benchmarks in our VPC without sending raw traces back.
04:30 - Speaker 1 (Alyssa Chen): Absolutely. Proposed measurement plan: 1) Baseline synthetic replay in Redwood hosted to validate tooling 2) Replay of anonymized traces in Redwood hosted 3) Private-run using same harness in your VPC 4) Final acceptance runs with traffic shaping and load sweep. We'll provide an open-source style harness (k6 + python runner + log exporter) and a spreadsheet for results.
04:55 - Speaker 4 (Dana Liu): For sampling: we can share one week of traces. How much data do you need to produce statistically meaningful p99?
05:05 - Speaker 3 (Mateo Ruiz): For p99, the rule of thumb is you need on the order of 10k+ tail samples for confidence; but because traces are correlated we plan to do block bootstrap and also synthetic augmentation. Practically, we'll run multiple sweep windows — e.g., 20k requests per bucket (short/med/long) to estimate tails.
05:25 - Speaker 1 (Alyssa Chen): We'll recommend default sample sizes in the template: 20k short, 20k med, 10k long, with at least three repeat runs at each load point. That gives a decent tail estimate and helps observe variability.
05:40 - Speaker 5 (Olivia Park): How do we account for cold caches and KV cache hits? Our real traffic has a good amount of prefix caching so cold-run numbers are pessimistic.
05:55 - Speaker 3 (Mateo Ruiz): Good point. We'll do two modes: cold-start run (no cache primed) and hot-run (with warmed prefix/KV cache). We'll capture both TTFT and TPOT for each. Also measure percent of requests served from cache to adjust expectations.
06:15 - Speaker 4 (Dana Liu): And batching effects — sometimes our request router batches to increase throughput; batching improves throughput but increases TTFT. We need to maintain tail SLOs when batching.
06:30 - Speaker 3 (Mateo Ruiz): Agreed. We'll include tests with batch sizes 1, 4, 8 and latency-oriented policy (no batching/low-latency) versus throughput policy. We'll capture tradeoff curves (latency vs tokens/sec).
06:46 - Speaker 2 (Samir): How about observability? We need per-token breakdown, model-run time, network, and queuing.
06:55 - Speaker 1 (Alyssa Chen): The harness emits timestamps: request arrive, request dispatch, model start, first token emit, token emits every n tokens, and final end. We'll include taggable metadata: model variant, quantization, hardware type. Redwood Console will provide dashboards but we'll also give CSVs you can keep locally.
07:15 - Speaker 6 (Jared Kim): Don't forget encryption and SSO access to logs.
07:20 - Speaker 1 (Alyssa Chen): We'll include role-based links and an export package.
07:25 - Speaker 5 (Olivia Park): Timeline?
07:28 - Speaker 1 (Alyssa Chen): Proposed three-week pilot: Week 0 (this week) prep and baseline; Week 1 hosted synthetic and initial tuning; Week 2 private runs and iterative tuning; Week 3 final acceptance sweep and handoff. Exact dates we'll coordinate after we get traces.
07:44 - Speaker 4 (Dana Liu): That timeline aligns with our internal release cycle. We want a pilot decision gate on week 3: either pass (move to Dedicated/Prod roll) or iterate with scope changes.
07:55 - Speaker 3 (Mateo Ruiz): Acceptance criteria we should record now: for medium-weighted distribution (60% med, 32% short, 8% long), meet customer thresholds: TTFT p95 <= 200ms and p99 <= 450ms; TPOT p95 <= 40ms and p99 <= 100ms on hosted. Private cluster bands: TTFT p95 <= 350ms, p99 <= 700ms; TPOT p95 <= 60ms, p99 <= 140ms. Also service must sustain the observed peak QPS for 30 minutes without error rate >0.5%.
08:28 - Speaker 2 (Samir): That seems fair. Will you include the exact measurement queries and SQL to compute p95/p99?
08:35 - Speaker 3 (Mateo Ruiz): Yes, the template includes clear aggregation queries and notes about bucketization, bootstrapping for tails, and how to tag outliers. We'll also include scripts that compute TTFT as (first_token_time - request_start_time) and TPOT as median inter-token delta after first token. The harness will emit everything in a structured CSV.
08:57 - Speaker 5 (Olivia Park): What about throughput metrics? We want tokens/sec and sustained RPS under a given latency envelope.
09:05 - Speaker 1 (Alyssa Chen): We'll include measurements: peak sustainable RPS at the latency envelope (e.g., RPS such that p95 TTFT < threshold), tokens/sec per GPU, cost estimate per 1M tokens for the config tested.
09:20 - Speaker 6 (Jared Kim): Security checklist again: audit log retention, KMS key rotation policy, and SOC2 artifacts.
09:30 - Speaker 1 (Alyssa Chen): We'll share security pack and SOC2 docs; for private runs we'll provide a minimal attestation and runbook.
09:40 - Speaker 4 (Dana Liu): Any concerns about sampling bias when we replay traces? We have a lot of bursts during the day — do you recommend time-of-day stratification?
09:50 - Speaker 3 (Mateo Ruiz): Yes — stratify by load windows: quiet, average, peak. We'll create synthetic bursts to simulate real diurnal spikes — e.g., ramp to peak QPS for 20 minutes. That helps expose queuing and autoscaling effects.
10:10 - Speaker 2 (Samir): For acceptance, can we also include a qualitative check — human-eval on first token quality under the low-latency policy? We don't want to sacrifice helpfulness for speed.
10:20 - Speaker 1 (Alyssa Chen): Good call. We'll add a small evaluation set (50 labeled prompts) to measure meaningful-first-token correctness and objectionable regression between model variants / quantization.
10:35 - Speaker 5 (Olivia Park): If Redwood recommends different quantization or smaller model variants for cost tradeoffs, we'll need a clear fallback plan for quality regression.
10:45 - Speaker 3 (Mateo Ruiz): We'll include A/B diffs and regression alerts; any quantization or distillation changes will be compared against the labeled set and a production-sampled set. Decision gate requires no more than 3% drop in helpfulness metrics on the labeled set.
11:00 - Speaker 4 (Dana Liu): Logging of the random seeds or determinism? We need reproducibility for debugging spikes.
11:08 - Speaker 1 (Alyssa Chen): Harness will include reproducibility flags and store full request/response IDs (anonymized) and model config snapshots.
11:20 - Speaker 6 (Jared Kim): For VPC runs, what connectivity windows are needed? We need minimal inbound exceptions.
11:28 - Speaker 4 (Dana Liu): Mark, can you confirm?
11:31 - Speaker 7 (Mark Rivera): I can open a temporary egress-only path for the harness to pull images and then we run locally; I'll coordinate with infra.
11:40 - Speaker 1 (Alyssa Chen): Great. To wrap up, recap of commitments: Alyssa sends template; Mateo and Priya will prepare test harness; Dana will send traces; Mark will schedule connectivity; we'll aim for initial hosted synthetic runs next week.
11:58 - Speaker 5 (Olivia Park): Quick micro decision: do we treat p95 TTFT as the main SLO and p99 as an alerting guardrail?
12:10 - Speaker 3 (Mateo Ruiz): Yes that is common. We'll label p95 as SLO and p99 as SLO guardrail with stricter escalation. We'll include both in the acceptance criteria table.
12:25 - Speaker 1 (Alyssa Chen): Any last questions?
12:30 - Speaker 2 (Samir): No, thanks — this is actionable.
12:34 - Speaker 1 (Alyssa Chen): Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the templates and schedule.

--- END TRANSCRIPT ---

NOTES: There are a few minor transcript mis-attrs (autogen). References to KV cache sometimes shows as "K V cash" in auto caption. Shared artifacts: https://redwood.example.com/benchmarks/template.csv (benchmark template), https://redwood.example.com/security/soc2-pack.pdf (security pack).
